sentences.text: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod characterized by a proportionally wide rib cage.
Its skull was proportionally larger and more robust than other sauropods, featuring powerful jaws capable of high bite forces.
The teeth were spoon-shaped, tilted forward, and rapidly replaced to process food.
Skin impressions have been found on at least one specimen, offering rare glimpses of its appearance.
The genus Camarasaurus was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
The type species of the genus is Camarasaurus supremus, which Cope named in the same year.
Other recognized species include C. grandis, named by Marsh in 1877; C. lentus, named by Marsh in 1889; and C. lewisi, named by Jensen in 1988.
Over 530 specimens of Camarasaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation in the western United States.
Camarasaurus was likely a selective feeder that browsed at heights ranging from 2 to 5 meters.
The hypothesis that Camarasaurus was semiaquatic was refuted in the 1970s, and it is now thought to have been entirely terrestrial.
Several Camarasaurus specimens show evidence of injury or disease, including bite marks and arthritis.
Camarasaurus is classified as a member of the sauropod group Macronaria.
Mook formally synonymized the genera Morosaurus and Camarasaurus in 1914.
John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined in 1996 that Cathetosaurus lewisi is a species of Camarasaurus, a view supported by most later studies.
Camarasaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages, between 155 and 143 million years ago.
It lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 155 to 145 million years ago, in what is now North America and France.
C. grandis lived during the Kimmeridgian, C. lentus during the late Kimmeridgian, and C. supremus during the Tithonian.
Camarasaurus lived in open conifer forests where hard-edible plants were abundant.
Some paleontologists have debated grouping Camarasaurus with genera like Tehuelchesaurus and Lourinhasaurus in the family Camarasauridae.
Marsh suggested in 1878 that Morosaurus was very sluggish in movement and had a brain proportionately smaller than any known vertebrate.
Henry Fairfield Osborn implied in 1898 that Atlantosaurus, Apatosaurus, Amphicoelias, and Brontosaurus were synonyms of Cope's Camarasaurus, a hypothesis that remains a subject of historical debate.
From 1901, papers suggested that Morosaurus and Camarasaurus might be the same genus, leading to their formal synonymization in 1914.
It is debated whether C. lentus is a distinct species, as its holotype is a juvenile found in the same locality as C. grandis and lacks diagnostic features.
